title: The quiet-above-ground change: it ran, and it is too small to see
question: Nothing to judge here -- this is me answering my own card. Do you want me to keep it, or should the near-surface rock lose its bedding entirely?
context_md:
You said the two panes of *'Layers starting deeper'* looked identical. That is a finding about the change, not about your eye, so I counted instead of guessing.

**It ran.** The two images are not the same file. It redraws **95,253 of 491,520 pixels -- 19.4% of the frame**. So it is not dead and it is not the wrong camera.

**And it is invisible because the change is tiny per pixel.** Where it changes anything, the colour moves by a **median of 11 out of 255**, mean 15, never more than 38. A fifth of the frame shifted by four percent of the range is not something anyone sees.

**The reason is structural.** The change swaps a bed's *tone* -- one of four shades inside one rock -- and those four shades are about 28 points apart by design. What you actually see between layers is the difference between *rocks*, and that is four times bigger. So unifying tone near the surface can never do what you asked; unifying the rock could, and that would mean the standing rock is one material rather than the bed it was cut from.

**That is the question.** I have not done it, because the differential erosion this world's new relief is made of depends on beds differing in strength, and I did not want to quietly weaken that to win a colour argument.

The picture is the current state -- the contrast drop from the other card, plus this.
